title: Falklands oil plans threaten seals, whales and penguins
content:
The Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, host significant oil reserves that are the subject of a sovereignty dispute between the two nations. Environmentalists express concern that these oil plans threaten one of the Atlantic’s richest ecosystems. The archipelago consists of East and West Falkland, along with 778 smaller islands and islets located east of Patagonia’s southern tip.

The region supports large colonies of albatrosses and penguins. Additionally, the waters surrounding the islands and the Patagonian shelf serve as feeding grounds for sea lions, southern elephant seals, and southern right whales.
summary: Environmentalists fear the Falklands oil plans could harm the islands' rich marine ecosystem. The Falklands, a British overseas territory claimed by Argentina, hosts large colonies of albatrosses, penguins, sea lions, southern elephant seals and southern right whales.
author: Guardian Business

title: US Thanksgiving Flights Hit by 18,000 Cancellations After FAA Ground Stop
content:
Millions of people are planning to fly in the United States for the Thanksgiving holiday, just two weeks after the Federal Aviation Administration implemented a nationwide ground stop on November 13. This event halted all flights for the first time since 9/11, excluding a brief halt in 2023. The disruption caused significant chaos, with some travelers driving overnight to reach cruise ships or purchasing new cars to attend business meetings, while others canceled their plans and incurred associated costs.

According to estimates from Anderson Economic Group, more than 18,000 flights were canceled during the incident. This resulted in a potential cost to travelers of $1.9 billion in lost time and related expenses. As the holiday travel period approaches, the article notes that travelers must navigate an outdated system and complex company policies in case of further disruptions, advising them to carry cash and know their rights.
summary: More than 18,000 flights were cancelled, costing travelers $1.9bn in lost time and expenses, according to Anderson Economic Group. The cancellations followed a 13 November FAA ground stop that halted all flights nationwide for the first time since 9/11.
author: Guardian Business

title: Global Stock Markets Volatile as AI Companies Face Sell-Offs
content:
Shares have been volatile amid growing jitters over technology and artificial‑intelligence companies. Investors are reportedly “getting cold feet” over the outlook for AI firms and are selling technology stocks, according to recent market reports.

Last week, the AI company Anthropic went public and recorded a record‑breaking first day on the exchange. However, on Friday global stock markets tumbled, and the U.S. Nasdaq closed 5 % below its previous level on 1 January.
summary: Global stock markets have seen rapid rallies and sharp sell-offs as investors grow wary of AI companies. The AI company Anthropic had a record-breaking first day after its launch, but markets fell and the US Nasdaq closed 5% lower on January 1.
author: Guardian Business

title: Nvidia Shares Close at $165.05 as CEO Jensen Huang Returns, Value Rises $950bn
content:
Nvidia’s market value surged by $950 billion after the company’s shares closed at $165.05, following the surprise reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang. The jump left the firm’s valuation still half a trillion dollars lower than before the affair was revealed.

President‑elect Donald Trump praised Huang, calling him a “great patriot and national treasure” in response to his return. The announcement generated widespread coverage in U.S. political circles, highlighting the CEO’s reinstatement as a key event in Nvidia’s recent timeline.

Meanwhile, UK housebuilder Crest Nicholson saw its shares fall by a quarter to a record low after issuing a profits warning. The company’s full‑year completions were 1,353, the bottom end of its guidance range of 1,350 to 1,400. The warning pushed Crest Nicholson shares down over 30%, dragging peers such as Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Vistry and Bellway into the red. The downturn reflects broader weakness in the housing market, affecting not only first‑time buyers but also affluent upsizers amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty.
summary: Nvidia Shares Close at $165.05 as CEO Jensen Huang Returns, Value Rises $950bn.
author: Guardian Business

title: Chernobyl‑surviving fungus could aid creation of nerve‑agent‑trapping materials
content:
Scientists have identified a fungus that can thrive in the Chernobyl exclusion zone and may be used to develop materials capable of trapping and breaking down nerve agents and pesticides.  

Deep inside the zone, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They are undeterred by the high radiation levels and, in some cases, grow toward the radiation.
summary: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides. Black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine and are undeterred by the radiation, some even growing toward it.
author: Phys.org

title: 40 Charred Papyrus Fragments Found in Thebes Reveal Widespread Curse Ritual
content:
A recent find of 40 charred papyrus fragments at a temple in the ancient city of Thebes has prompted scholars to rethink a well‑known ancient Egyptian curse ritual.  

The fragments suggest the ritual was far more widespread and commonplace than previously believed, altering researchers’ understanding of its historical reach.
summary: Researchers discovered 40 charred papyrus fragments at a temple in Thebes. The fragments suggest that the famous ancient Egyptian curse ritual was more widespread and commonplace than previously thought.
author: Phys.org

title: Automated AI pollen analysis matches conventional honey testing
content: A research team from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) and the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) in Leipzig has developed an automated, AI‑based pollen analysis method for honey testing. The method was created in collaboration with several partners and is designed to assess the pollen content of single‑flower honeys, which must contain a specific proportion of pollen from the plant that produced the nectar. According to the project’s findings, the automated analysis closely matches conventional testing, offering a faster and less expert‑dependent alternative for verifying honey authenticity.
summary: A research team from the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research (UFZ) and the German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) in Leipzig developed an automated AI-based pollen analysis method for honey testing. The new method closely matches conventional pollen analysis results used to verify the pollen content of single-flower honeys.
author: Phys.org

title: HD 158485 Revealed as Pulsating Binary in JWST Calibration Sample
content:
Stars used to calibrate the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) require precisely characterized spectra to ensure accurate flux measurements. However, some stars that appear single can actually host unresolved companions that alter their predicted radiation output. 

Recent observations have revealed that HD 158485, an A‑type star in the JWST calibration program, is not a single star but a binary system. Both components of the binary exhibit pulsations, a detail that could affect the star’s spectral profile used for calibration.
summary: Stars used to calibrate JWST must have precisely characterized spectra for accurate flux measurements. The A‑type star HD 158485 in the JWST calibration program has now been shown to be a binary system whose two stars both pulsate, showing that unresolved companions can alter predicted radiation.
author: Phys.org

title: Half of world speaks multiple languages, but proficiency levels vary widely
content: Roughly half of the world’s population speaks more than one language. The source notes that fluency in two or three languages differs markedly from claiming proficiency in five, ten or more, highlighting a distinction between modest multilingual ability and the broader skill set associated with being a polyglot.
summary: Roughly half of the world's population speaks more than one language. Speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.
author: Phys.org

title: Review finds chaotic patchwork of data center rules in all 50 states
content:
A recent policy review has uncovered a “chaotic” patchwork of rules governing data centers in all 50 states. The findings highlight the lack of uniform standards across the country.

The artificial‑intelligence boom has sparked debates over where data centers should be located, how large they can become, and how to ensure that local communities benefit from them. These discussions reflect the broader uncertainty about the best regulatory approach.

At the core of the debate is whether state and local governments should ban data centers outright, welcome them with open arms, or adopt a middle‑ground strategy.
summary: A review of data center policies found a chaotic patchwork of rules in every state. The artificial intelligence boom has sparked debates over where data centers will be located, how large they should be, how communities can benefit, and whether governments should ban, welcome, or regulate them.
author: Phys.org

title: Ancient human settlements boosted biomass of today’s Amazon rainforest
content: Rainforest areas with a history of human occupation possess, on average, 2.8 percent greater biomass than untouched regions. This finding suggests that previous assessments of Amazonian biomass may have been slightly overestimated, as they primarily evaluated formerly occupied areas.
summary: Ancient human settlements boosted biomass of today’s Amazon rainforest.
author: New Scientist

title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
content: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries. Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas. The secret weapon that could finally force climate action What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.” Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement. But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process? The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision. With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful. The looming El Niño could be bad – but much worse is to come But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says. The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says. There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable. UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.
summary: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus.
author: New Scientist

title: Scientists explore overlooked nutrients that may delay aging
content: A recent hypothesis suggests that some nutrients in food may not only support basic survival but also delay aging. Researchers are actively working to identify these specific longevity nutrients and understand their age‑delaying effects.
summary: A hypothesis suggests some food nutrients may have age‑delaying effects beyond basic survival. Researchers are working to identify these longevity nutrients.
author: New Scientist

title: J-PAL North America Launches Medicaid Learning Lab for State Agency Evaluation
content:
J-PAL North America, the regional office of MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab, has launched the Medicaid Learning Lab (MLL) in collaboration with the SCALE Lab at the Yale School of Public Health. This fully funded program, which runs through April 2027, supports an inaugural cohort of four state Medicaid agencies: the Delaware Department of Health and Social Services, the Louisiana Department of Health, MassHealth, and TennCare. The initiative is designed to help these agencies test, learn, and improve health care delivery by utilizing evidence to determine effective programs and directing resources toward initiatives with proven impact.

A September kickoff convening brought together more than 20 Medicaid leaders, researchers, and collaborators, serving as the first in-person meeting before the program’s online sessions began. Speakers included Amy Finkelstein, co-scientific director of J-PAL North America and the John and Jennie S. MacDonald Professor of Economics at MIT; Jacob Wallace of Yale University, scientific advisor to the MLL and faculty co-director of the SCALE Lab; and Rebecca Myerson, associate professor at Emory University. Practitioners also presented, including Bill Halsey, director of healthcare policy and innovation at the Connecticut Department of Social Services; Allison Espeseth of Covering Wisconsin; and Hannah Maniates, director of Medicaid programming at the National Association of Medicaid Directors.

Halsey highlighted the importance of a test-and-learn mentality, noting that rigorous evaluation methodologies established before implementation can generate actionable insights in a shorter time frame compared to post-implementation evaluations. Maniates identified common questions agencies bring to researchers, such as the effectiveness of member outreach, strategies for automatic renewals, and the impact of enrollment changes on utilization. Finkelstein traced the inspiration for the MLL to the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment, which she led, arguing that programs of Medicaid’s consequence should not rely on accidental budget constraints to generate randomized evidence.

The MLL addresses common evaluation challenges, including a lack of standard frameworks, cost-benefit mismatches, and difficulties in establishing researcher partnerships. Participating agencies will receive individualized technical assistance from J-PAL staff to identify evaluation ideas and develop preliminary randomized evaluation designs. Each team will work to prioritize a specific program, develop a theory of change, and outline a randomization plan, informed by a forthcoming playbook co-developed by the SCALE Lab and J-PAL North America. Selected agencies will be connected with J-PAL network researchers to co-develop evaluation concepts, with projects eligible for funding awards of up to $400,000 from J-PAL’s Health Care Delivery Initiative.

This program is the latest iteration of J-PAL North America’s Learning Lab model, following the Climate Action Learning Lab and the AprendeLab in Puerto Rico. It builds on prior work launching randomized evaluations in South Carolina, Wisconsin, Connecticut, and Maine. Wallace noted that Connecticut’s sustained partnership with Yale researchers, which began with a single evaluation of adolescent vaccination outreach, demonstrates the potential trajectory for MLL participants. The program will conclude with a summit next spring where each team will present its evaluation opportunity. The MLL is made possible through a grant from Arnold Ventures.
summary: J-PAL North America Launches Medicaid Learning Lab for State Agency Evaluation.
author: MIT News

title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years amid vaccine myths
content:
The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years.  

A new survey shows widespread misconceptions about the disease and its vaccine.  More than one‑third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine‑autism link, and most respondents do not know the risks of measles or how many vaccine doses children need.
summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years as cases rise. A new survey shows that over one‑third of Americans still believe or are unsure about the debunked vaccine‑autism link and most do not know the disease’s risks or the number of vaccine doses children need.
author: Science Daily

title: Galactic shock wave may trigger star formation in Milky Way
content:
Scientists have reported a discovery indicating that the Milky Way is forming stars in locations where most galaxies do not. Evidence points to a massive rotating structure near the galactic center that generates powerful shock waves, which appear to trigger rather than suppress star formation.

In addition, researchers suggest that a segment of the Norma spiral arm may not be a true spiral arm; instead, it could be a large region dominated by newly born stars. This finding could alter current understandings of the galaxy’s structure.
summary: Scientists discovered a massive rotating structure near the Milky Way's center that creates powerful shock waves, which trigger star formation instead of suppressing it. The discovery also suggests that part of the Norma spiral arm may be a vast star‑forming region rather than a traditional spiral arm.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists Find Unknown Viruses That Could Explain Early Life Evolution
content: Scientists have identified previously unknown viruses that may illuminate how some of the earliest biological structures evolved. The discovery challenges a longstanding evolutionary theory and indicates that viruses could possess functions beyond merely infecting cells, suggesting broader, hidden capabilities in viral biology.
summary: Scientists discovered previously unknown viruses that may explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists shut brain cells, mice sleep 70% less
content: Scientists have identified brain cells that generate the irresistible urge to sleep. By shutting these cells down, mice slept 70 % less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, suggesting intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.
summary: Scientists discovered brain cells that generate the urge to sleep and found that shutting them down let mice sleep 70% less than normal. Many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising possibilities for future sleep research.
author: Science Daily

title: Archaeologists say Iron Age ruler Verica was a woman
content:
Archaeologists uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman.  

The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.
summary: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.
author: Science Daily

title: Two monster black holes from the dawn of time defy explanation
content: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants grew to sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.
summary: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, powered by two enormous black holes that existed just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Weighing an astonishing 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, these cosmic giants somehow grew to incredible sizes far earlier than current theories can explain.
author: Science Daily

title: California trapdoor spider named for Stephen Colbert has genome 50% larger than human
content:
A tiny California trapdoor spider, named after Stephen Colbert, has a genome that is roughly 50 % larger than a human’s. The spider, about the size of a quarter, contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes.

Scientists discovered the spider’s large genome, which provides surprising clues about spider evolution.
summary: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's despite being about the size of a quarter. Scientists found the spider’s genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, offering clues to spider evolution.
author: Science Daily

title: Japanese researchers develop egg yolk antibody and near‑infrared light gum treatment
content: Researchers in Japan have created a gum‑disease treatment that pairs egg‑yolk antibodies with near‑infrared light to destroy harmful bacteria while leaving beneficial microbes unharmed. The approach, unlike conventional therapies, preserves the mouth’s natural bacterial balance and protects healthy gum cells, and it markedly reduced bone loss from periodontitis in mouse studies.
summary: Researchers in Japan created a gum disease treatment that uses egg yolk antibodies and near‑infrared light to kill harmful bacteria while sparing beneficial microbes. In mice, the treatment significantly reduced bone loss associated with periodontitis.
author: Science Daily

title: Cop31 climate talks end in failure as deal omits fossil fuel language
content: The latest COP climate conference, described as the longest ever, concluded without an agreement as participating nations could not reach a deal. Organizers noted that the final draft omitted any reference to fossil fuels, which was identified as the principal obstacle to consensus. In a related podcast, Madeleine Finlay interviews Guardian environment editor Fiona Harvey, who reported from Antalya, Turkey, about the negotiations and discusses possible next steps. Listeners are invited to view Reuters clips and complete a podcast survey.
summary: The longest ever Cop climate talks in Antalya, Turkey concluded without an agreement as countries could not reach a deal. The stalemate centered on the final draft’s omission of any mention of fossil fuels, discussed in a podcast with Guardian environment editor Fiona Harvey and Madeleine Finlay.
author: Guardian Science

title: Warming winters and extreme weather threaten Wisconsin's cranberry harvest
content:
Scientists are racing to identify and breed new berry varieties that can thrive on an increasingly warmer planet. In rural Wisconsin, harvest time has turned the landscape a vivid red as the state’s cranberry crop—responsible for more than 60 % of the nation’s supply—is gathered. For nearly three decades, farmer Nicole Hansen has cultivated cranberries in the Badger State, and on a crisp fall morning she and a reporter waded into a marsh to round up the floating harvest.

The report comes from Climate Central, an independent group of scientists and communicators that researches and reports how a changing climate affects people’s lives.
summary: Scientists are racing to identify and breed new cranberry varieties that can thrive as winters warm and extreme weather increases. Wisconsin, which supplies more than 60% of the nation’s cranberries, is home to longtime farmer Nicole Hansen who harvests the crop in the state’s marshes.
author: Guardian Science

title: Webb Maps Cassiopeia A Dust, Revealing Pre‑Supernova Shell Merger
content:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has produced a detailed mid‑infrared view of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A (Cas A), revealing the hot dust that fills the nebula and offering new clues about the structure of the star that exploded. The high‑resolution observation, captured with Webb’s MIRI instrument, was described in a study published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

The Webb data show that the dust composition varies across the remnant, indicating a dramatic change in the star’s interior shortly before its death. The authors interpret the findings as evidence of a “shell merger,” in which layers inside the star mixed together hours before the supernova. Lead author Tea Temim, a research scientist at Columbia University, explained that the merger of the oxygen‑ and carbon‑burning shells would alter the star’s structure and the chemical abundances seen in the ejecta.

To target the most informative regions, the team first used archival observations from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope, which identified three key areas for Webb to examine. Two of those sites lie within Cas A’s reverse‑shocked region; one contains mostly silica dust while the other is dominated by carbon dust. The third target, dubbed the “Green Monster,” was found to be rich in complex magnesium silicates and originates from material the star shed before the explosion, rather than from the supernova ejecta.

The dust map was further refined by incorporating X‑ray data from NASA’s Chandra Observatory and the JAXA‑led XRISM mission. Co‑author Dan Milisavljevic, an associate professor at Purdue University, noted that Webb’s ability to resolve individual, solar‑system‑sized clumps enables a more sophisticated analysis of dust chemistry, allowing researchers to link the present‑day remnant back to the progenitor star’s final hours. The merger signatures appear throughout much of the remnant, suggesting a widespread mixing event just before core collapse.

These results illustrate how Webb’s unprecedented resolution and sensitivity are opening new pathways for astronomers to infer the internal histories of massive stars by studying the dust they leave behind. Webb, an international program led by NASA with partners ESA and CSA, continues to provide insights into stellar evolution, the origins of elements, and the enrichment of future generations of stars and planets.
summary: Webb Maps Cassiopeia A Dust, Revealing Pre‑Supernova Shell Merger.
author: NASA News

title: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space
content:
The NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept” invites viewers to follow the Europa Clipper spacecraft from its conception to its current deep‑space operations. The film will air on NASA+, the NASA app, and the agency’s website beginning Monday, Nov. 23, and will soon appear on YouTube. The documentary is a behind‑the‑scenes look at the mission that has taken the largest NASA spacecraft into deep space.

Europa Clipper launched from Kennedy Space Center on Oct. 14, 2024, and is now two years into its five‑year, 1.8 billion‑mile (2.9 billion‑kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system. The orbiter will conduct flybys of Europa to determine whether the moon’s subsurface ocean contains the ingredients for life. The mission’s nine science instruments were built to survive the intense radiation produced by Jupiter’s magnetic field, a condition that may also help create a habitable environment beneath Europa’s icy surface.

The documentary traces the scientific lineage that led to Europa Clipper. Galileo Galilei first discovered the moon in 1610, and NASA’s Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 missions in 1973 and 1974 provided the first data. Voyager 1’s 1979 flyby gave the first detailed images, followed by Voyager 2, Galileo, Cassini, and Juno missions that each added new insights and paved the way for the current mission. Work on Europa Clipper officially began at Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in 2013, launching an 11‑year effort to design the spacecraft and its instruments for a launch window defined by planetary alignment.

The film also highlights the challenges faced by the team, including a global pandemic and a Category 5 hurricane and tornadoes near Kennedy Space Center just before launch. “With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration,” said Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s former project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.”

“The Europa Concept” showcases the thousands of engineers, scientists, and support staff who brought Europa Clipper to the launch pad and who will share the mission’s discoveries in the coming years. The documentary is available on NASA+ at https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/. For additional information about the mission, visit https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/. Media contact: Matthew Segal, Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 818‑354‑8307, matthew.j.segal@nasa.gov.
summary: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space.
author: NASA News

title: NASA seeks partners for first Moon nuclear reactor
content:
NASA is soliciting industry partners to design and test Lunar Reactor-1 (LR-1), the first nuclear reactor intended to provide electricity on the Moon. This small fission power system is designed to generate 20 kilowatts of electricity, a capacity equivalent to powering approximately 16 average U.S. households annually on Earth. The agency aims to have a launch-ready system by 2030 and to operate it on the lunar surface for at least five years after deployment.

The reactor is intended to support future lunar infrastructure, including habitats, communications systems, rovers, and scientific instruments. Unlike solar power, which is unavailable during the Moon’s approximately two-week-long nights, a nuclear reactor provides continuous electricity. This capability is crucial for operations in areas with limited or no sunlight. Brian Giblin, NASA’s Lunar Reactor-1 program manager, stated that a reliable source of safe and abundant energy is vital for future exploration of the lunar and Martian surfaces, allowing NASA assets to operate without dependency on sunlight.

NASA’s Space Power and Reactor Capabilities Request for Proposals incorporates feedback from a draft proposal released in August and an industry day held in September at the Ohio Aerospace Institute in Cleveland. Proposals are due by December 21. The solicitation requires the reactor to meet Department of Energy (DOE) safety standards for nuclear operations. While the primary focus is on advancing LR-1’s technology and flight design, NASA may issue additional task orders to support the development of other space nuclear power systems.

LR-1 is managed by NASA’s Space Reactors Division in partnership with the DOE. The division is also responsible for the Space Reactor‑1 (SR-1) Freedom, which is scheduled to launch in 2028. SR-1 Freedom will deliver three SkyFall helicopters to Mars and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion, a system that uses reactor-generated electricity to power spacecraft propulsion. These technologies are designed to enable deeper space missions that are not feasible with conventional propulsion methods.
summary: NASA is soliciting industry proposals to develop Lunar Reactor-1, a 20-kilowatt fission power system intended to sustain human presence on the Moon. The agency aims to have the launch-ready system operational by 2030 to provide continuous power during lunar nights.
author: NASA News

title: Studying Cancer Cells in Microgravity
content:
Encapsulate Inc. released an image taken on Nov. 19, 2026 that shows gastric microtumors grown within the company’s biochip. The image accompanies the Encapsulate‑1 investigation, which is analyzing patient‑derived tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to examine how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity.

According to the release, findings from the study could enable further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments. The International Space Station, orbiting more than 200 miles (320 km) above Earth, is described as a hub for cutting‑edge science that enables discoveries not possible on Earth. Image credit: Encapsulate Inc.
summary: Studying Cancer Cells in Microgravity.
author: NASA News

title: NASA awards $290.6 million Northrop Grumman contract for NOAA NEON microwave sounders
content:
NASA has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave‑Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The hybrid cost‑plus‑fixed‑fee, firm‑fixed‑price, and time‑and‑materials contract is valued at $290.6 million and covers a period of performance from November 23 to April 1, 2042. The work will be performed at the awardee’s facility.

Under the agreement, Northrop Grumman will design, develop, produce, test, and provide mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next‑generation low‑Earth‑orbit microwave sounders. NOAA will own and operate the instruments and deliver the resulting data to users worldwide. The microwave sounders will measure atmospheric temperature and moisture, data that are critical for weather pattern analysis and could improve medium‑range forecasts for NOAA’s National Weather Service.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the acquisition, while NOAA leads the NEON mission, providing funding, technical requirements, and post‑launch operations. NASA will manage satellite development and launch, and both agencies will collaborate with commercial partners to design and build the NEON spacecraft and instruments.

For additional information about NASA and agency programs, visit https://www.nasa.gov. Contact Liz Vlock, Headquarters, Washington, 202‑358‑1600, liz.vlock@nasa.gov; or Peter Jacobs, Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, 301‑286‑3308, peter.jacobs@nasa.gov.
summary: Credit: NASA NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder for Microwave-Based Applications (SMBA) instruments on NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network (NEON) satellites. The cost-plus-fixed-fee, firm-fixed-price, and time-and-materials hybrid contract has a value of $290.6 million.
author: NASA News

title: NariQ delivers BF16‑level performance with 3‑bit quantization of Qwen3.8‑27B
content:
Nari Labs announced the release of NariQ, a set of 3‑bit‑or‑lower quantizations for the Qwen3.8‑27B model that aim to preserve BF16‑level performance. According to the developers, the quantizations maintain near‑BF16 quality on a range of tasks, including agentic operations, mathematics, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding. They note that this is the first quantization at this bit depth to retain BF16‑level results on long‑horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmark scores are presented for BF16, 3‑bit, 2.5‑bit, and 2‑bit versions across several tests: DeepSWE (39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6), Terminal‑Bench 2.1 (62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4), AIME 25+26 (97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0), MSGM (94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6), and RealWorldQA (82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9). Decode speed is reported as comparable to other quantizations when run on an RTX PRO 6000 GPU.

Context‑length performance is also listed, with scores for 4K, 16K, and 64K token windows: 3‑bit (88.9 / 84.5 / 70.7), 2.5‑bit (99.2 / 93.8 / 77.5), 2‑bit (111.7 / 105.1 / 85.0), and an Unsloth UD‑IQ3_XXS baseline (94.7 / 89.8 / 74.8). The quantizations currently require the Nari‑labs fork of llama.cpp, available at https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp. The team invites feedback and questions via a Hacker News discussion linked in the announcement.
summary: We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding. To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.
author: Hacker News

title: AI models excel at coding but lag on judgment; rock weathering may curb crop yields
content:
The latest edition of The Download highlights two pressing concerns in the technology sector. First, an updated report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR reveals that while certain AI capabilities are improving exponentially, models still lag on tasks that require judgment. The report revises METR’s widely shared time‑horizon plot, which originally tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open‑ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments. According to the report, models struggled with these tasks, a weakness that could prove crucial to automating research and development. The newsletter invites readers to explore where AI progress is encountering tougher challenges.

Second, the newsletter turns to carbon removal and its potential impact on agriculture. Google, Microsoft, and other companies are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups that spread crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air—a process known as enhanced rock weathering. The approach is said to improve soil quality and boost crop yields. However, new research reported exclusively by MIT Technology Review raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it begins to reduce yields. The findings suggest that the carbon‑removal potential of enhanced rock weathering could be far smaller than previously estimated, prompting major concerns about the feasibility of the technique.

These two stories underscore the limits of current AI systems in handling complex, judgment‑based tasks and the environmental trade‑offs of emerging carbon‑removal technologies. Both developments highlight the need for careful evaluation as the technology industry pushes forward.
summary: AI models excel at coding but lag on judgment; rock weathering may curb crop yields.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Thomas Nagel Criticizes Anthropic's AI Consciousness Claim
content: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well. Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm. This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious). But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place. Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer. You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models. The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences. But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “ terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet. Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?” It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing. Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place. Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement. But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process. Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.
summary: Thomas Nagel publicly rebuked Anthropic's view that AI models could be conscious, arguing that language production alone does not prove consciousness and that silicon-based systems differ fundamentally from biological brains. His comments followed Anthropic's recent risk disclosure that AI sentience might require additional safeguards for investors.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Pete Hegseth’s DC church led by Idaho pastor Doug Wilson draws Pentagon officials
content: A radical Washington, D.C., church associated with Pete Hegseth is drawing senior government figures. The congregation, founded by Idaho pastor Doug Wilson—who seeks to repeal women’s right to vote—opened in the capital last year and now includes top officials from the Pentagon and across the government.
summary: Doug Wilson, an Idaho pastor who wants to repeal women’s right to vote, set up shop in DC last year. Now his congregation boasts top officials from the Pentagon and throughout the government.

title: Livestream on Dec 2 to Discuss AI Safety and Industry Response
content: Experts say AI presents a real danger in some form. A livestream scheduled for December 2 will allow participants to submit questions about whether the industry will act to keep users safe from AI, with answers provided during the event.
summary: Experts agree that AI poses real danger. A livestream on December 2 will answer audience questions about industry action on AI safety.

title: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO
content: Nvidia’s board of directors has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive officer. The reinstatement comes a little more than a week after Huang resigned amid allegations that he engaged in multiple affairs, including one with a direct report.
summary: Nvidia’s board of directors reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. He had resigned a little more than a week earlier amid allegations of multiple affairs, including with a direct report.

content: The U.S. Army intends to detonate 9,500 pounds of lead azide stored at an ammunition plant in Iowa. Local officials said they learned most of the details about the operation from a press release.

title: Nothing unveils Ear Note AI transcription earbuds ahead of Dec. 8 launch
content:
Nothing’s upcoming Ear Note is a pair of earbuds that come with a microphone‑equipped charging case capable of recording and transcribing conversations. The device pairs with a connected app that lets users manage recordings, transcriptions and AI‑generated summaries, a functionality the report likens to Apple’s new Watch feature and Amazon’s Bee wearable.

CEO Carl Pei demonstrated the Ear Note to Bloomberg and said the company has not yet set a price, with a launch planned for December 8. The same report notes that rumored plans for an AI smartwatch and smart glasses have been delayed, while Nothing intends to pursue a more aggressive smartphone release schedule next year.
summary: Nothing unveils Ear Note AI transcription earbuds ahead of Dec. 8 launch.
