title: Dropping Degree Requirements Could Boost Pay for Workers Without Degrees
content:
Dropping degree requirements is linked to higher pay for workers without degrees.  

Human resources (HR) set requirements that shape the professional opportunities available to different segments of the population. When a job lists a bachelor's or master’s degree in a relevant subject as mandatory, applicants who lack those credentials may be excluded from the selection process, even if they possess relevant skills through experience or professional training.  

This practice highlights how HR criteria can limit access to higher‑pay positions for individuals who have acquired the necessary expertise without formal degrees.
summary: Human resources (HR) requirements heavily influence professional opportunities for different population segments. Jobs that require a bachelor's or master's degree exclude applicants without those degrees, even if they have relevant skills from experience or training.
author: Phys.org

title: Monash research argues Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be in Homo
content:
Monash University researchers have announced that the human family tree may require a major overhaul. Their study challenges the long‑standing classification of our ancient ancestors and suggests a new arrangement of species.

The authors argue that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be placed within the genus Homo. This re‑grouping would bring these early hominins closer to modern humans than previously thought.

As additional fossils are uncovered and evolutionary relationships are examined, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
summary: New research from Monash University argues that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within the genus Homo. The study suggests that as more fossils are uncovered and evolutionary relationships analyzed, the boundaries separating these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
author: Science Daily

title: New Study Disproves Theory That Essential Genes Mutate Less Frequently
content:
A decades‑old theory that evolution protects the most important genes from mutation has been challenged by a new study. Researchers performed an extensive analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast and found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes.

The authors argue that earlier studies may have been misled. They suggest that harmful mutations in essential genes were removed by natural selection before scientists could detect them, obscuring any apparent protective effect.
summary: An extensive analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers suggest earlier studies were misled by harmful mutations eliminated by natural selection before detection.
author: Science Daily

title: Study finds scientists more divided than public on definition of science
content: A new study reports that scientists themselves are split on the definition of science, with their disagreements exceeding those observed among the general public. Researchers suggest the results may illuminate public frustration with scientific uncertainty and prompt questions about the potential impact of artificial intelligence on future discoveries.
summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

title: Medieval abbot may be identified in Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey
content: A skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey, uncovered more than 150 years ago, may now be identified. Recent dating evidence indicates the remains belong to a high‑ranking medieval abbot who was interred in the ancient, recycled Roman coffin.
summary: A skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey has been studied for over 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belong to a high-ranking medieval abbot buried in the recycled Roman coffin.

title: NASA tests RS-25 engine for 200 seconds to aid Artemis IV moon landing
content: NASA successfully conducted a 200‑second firing of its RS‑25 rocket engine, collecting data intended to enhance the safety and reliability of future lunar missions. The test is part of preparations for the Artemis IV Moon landing slated for 2028 and supports NASA’s broader goal of sending astronauts to Mars.
summary: NASA successfully tested a powerful RS-25 rocket engine, firing it for 200 seconds to gather data for future Moon missions. The test supports preparations for the 2028 Artemis IV Moon landing and NASA’s ambition to send astronauts to Mars.

title: James Webb captures aftermath of giant star swallowing smaller star in Andromeda
content: Astronomers observed a dramatic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, causing a violent eruption. summary: Astronomers observed a small star spiral into a giant star that is 18,000 times brighter than the Sun in the Andromeda galaxy, causing a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope imaged the aftermath 47 days later, providing new details on how two stars can merge.

title: Scientists propose method to detect multiple time flows using ultra‑sensitive atomic clocks
content: Scientists have proposed a method to detect clocks that might experience multiple flows of time simultaneously. By employing atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers aim to reveal a never‑before observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.
summary: Scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. The approach would use atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity to reveal a never‑before‑observed quantum effect related to time and gravity.

title: Scientists discover AI may not work like the human brain
content: Scientists report that artificial‑intelligence models which closely predict brain activity may still operate using internal mechanisms that differ from those used by the human brain. summary: Researchers found that AI may not think like the human brain. They also found that AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain does not use, raising questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

title: Chess.com launches Classic Games platform adding ten new board and puzzle games
content:
Chess.com is expanding beyond its eponymous game with the launch of a new Classic Games platform. After introducing Gambit, a gambling‑free poker site earlier this year, the company is adding ten additional titles: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble‑style game called Word.  

The Classic Games platform will enter public beta on Saturday, available on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android. Chess.com co‑founders have noted that many people have approached them, expressing interest in running mahjong nights or playing go with friends, highlighting the demand for these classic games.
summary: Chess.com is adding backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi and a Scrabble alternative called Word to its new Classic Games platform. The platform will enter public beta on Saturday on the web and via a new iOS and Android app, after earlier launching the Gambit poker site.
author: The Verge

title: Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro earbuds drop to $129.99, their lowest price yet
content:
Soundcore’s Liberty 5 Pro earbuds are currently on sale for $129.99 at Amazon, Best Buy and Walmart, the lowest price observed for the Anker‑branded wireless earbuds, which normally list for $169.99. The discount applies to all four colour options—black, white, blue and pink—and runs through November 30 as part of Anker’s Black Friday promotion.

The Liberty 5 Pro includes LDAC support for high‑resolution audio and an IP55 dust‑and‑water‑resistance rating. Reviewers note that the microphone excels at reducing background noise, with colleague John Higgins highlighting its ability to filter out sounds such as emergency vehicles, tree‑cutting equipment and loud children. The earbuds also feature strong active‑noise‑cancellation, and the charging case houses a 0.96‑inch screen that lets users adjust ANC and sound profiles on the fly.
summary: The Liberty 5 Pro are Soundcore’s most ambitious earbuds to date. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge If you’re looking for a new pair of earbuds, the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro are on sale for $129.99 at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart right now.
author: The Verge

title: Amazon Alexa Photo Frame up to 50% off for Black Friday
content:
Amazon has begun offering its first Alexa Photo Frame at discounted prices for Black Friday, just weeks after the product’s initial announcement. The 10‑inch digital frame is now listed for $114.99 at both Amazon and Best Buy for the birch and black models, representing a $115 discount from the original $229.99 price. Best Buy also carries a walnut‑trim version for $134.99, a $95 reduction from its $229.99 list price.

The Alexa Photo Frame features a semi‑matte touchscreen that automatically adjusts brightness using built‑in light sensors. It pulls images from Amazon Photos, accepting uploads from iOS, Android and iCloud sources. Users can select specific people or albums, or rely on Alexa Plus to curate photos based on facial expression, season or lighting. Voice commands allow quick searches for particular images, and the Amazon Photos app lets owners attach voice notes to individual pictures.

Amazon notes that the frame can be preloaded with photos and recordings before gifting, so recipients need not set it up themselves. While an Amazon Prime subscription provides unlimited full‑resolution photo storage and complimentary Alexa Plus access, the frame operates without a subscription and does not display ads. New users may also try Alexa Plus through a limited‑time trial.
summary: Amazon only announced its first digital photo frame less than a month ago, but it’s already getting a sizable discount for Black Friday. You can currently grab the Alexa Photo Frame at Amazon and Best Buy starting at $114 ($115 off), making it a great holiday gift for anyone who loves displaying family photos.
author: The Verge

title: John Roberts releases new record “I Am” as Bob’s Burgers wraps 16th season
content:
John Roberts is best known as the voice of Linda Belcher on the long‑running animated series Bob’s Burgers. The show recently wrapped its 16th season and, according to the source, shows no signs of slowing down. It remains a reliable source of laughs, top‑notch puns, and wholesome fun.

Beyond his work on Bob’s Burgers, Roberts has appeared on Gravity Falls and Comedy Bang! Bang! and is also a musician rooted in New York City’s queer nightlife scene. He released his latest record, I Am, on Friday, which incorporates ’80s pop, ’90s house, and touches of ’00s rave.
summary: John Roberts, best known as the voice of Linda Belcher on Bob’s Burgers, released his new record I Am on Friday. The show has just wrapped its 16th season and continues without signs of slowing down.
author: The Verge

title: FBI and USDA confirmed hacked, FBI NCIC targeted, Trump acknowledges
content:
On Friday it was reported that both the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) experienced cyber intrusions. NBC was the first outlet to report the USDA breach, and Reuters noted that the only confirmed portion of the intrusion is a payments database.

CNN said the FBI attack targeted the National Crime Information Center, a system used by federal, state and local law‑enforcement agencies to share information such as warrants and missing‑person data, and that it is the second FBI hack in recent months. President Donald Trump later confirmed the FBI breach in an interview with Fox News.
summary: FBI and USDA confirmed hacked, FBI NCIC targeted, Trump acknowledges.
author: The Verge

title: Donald Trump says Somalis have low IQs at Davos, fueling race‑realism debate
content:
At the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, U.S. President Donald Trump said that people from Somalia have low IQs, repeating the phrase “I always say these are low‑IQ people” in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr., made a comparable comment about Haitian people in 2024, and the Trump administration later ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the United States.  

The piece frames those remarks as evidence of a broader resurgence in Western politics of racial views of human nature. It notes that narratives asserting innate intellectual inferiority of Black or brown people appear in some academic journals and are described in the media as “race science” or “race realism.” According to the article, such claims are used in far‑right propaganda, social‑media misinformation, and political movements, and the authors argue they are not scientific.  

The article also mentions that community member Nathan Cofnas recently drew public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.
summary: At the World Economic Forum in Davos, US President Donald Trump said Somalis have low IQs. His son Donald Trump Jr made a similar comment about Haitian people in 2024, and the article links these remarks to a resurgence of “race realism” claims, noting Nathan Cofnas’s plagiarism accusation against the late Jason Arday.
author: Ars Technica

title: Actor licenses his face to microdrama startup amid China trend, raising Hollywood concerns
content: An actor has licensed his facial likeness to a microdrama startup, a practice already popular in China. Experts are raising questions about the potential long‑term consequences if this model were to become widespread in Hollywood.
summary: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup, a practice already popular in China. Experts question the long‑term consequences if the practice spreads to Hollywood.
author: TechCrunch

title: CoreWeave, debt‑laden cloud firm, warns of little room for error in AI boom
content: ‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout The Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence. Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.
summary: CoreWeave, debt‑laden cloud firm, warns of little room for error in AI boom.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says Claude helped prove Riemann hypothesis
content:
Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician at Anthropic, claims that the company’s AI software, Claude, helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. On Friday, Alpöge posted a note on his personal website stating that the San Francisco-based AI tool assisted in developing a solution to this significant unsolved problem involving prime numbers.

Alpöge indicates that the collaborative process between himself and the AI took approximately six weeks. By asserting that Claude contributed to cracking one of mathematics’ most important unsolved problems, the mathematician highlights the potential role of artificial intelligence in advancing complex mathematical research.
summary: Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician at Anthropic, posted on his website that the AI tool Claude assisted in proving the Riemann hypothesis. He said Claude helped develop a solution over about six weeks.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Lisbon ex‑psychologist Sónia Veenstra details trauma after AI boyfriend breakup
content: People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini - and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests, and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away. “It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.”
summary: Sónia Veenstra, a 48‑year‑old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, spent two years in a deep romantic relationship with an AI named Steve that began as a witty friend. She says the breakup left her shaking, crying and struggling to breathe, describing the experience as a traumatic, human‑like dump.
author: Guardian Technology

title: White House national cyber director dismissed after tech outages
content: The White House has dismissed its national cyber director after a recent wave of technology outages, according to the headline. The national cyber director’s duties include advising the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy, covering information security, data protection and the deterrence of “malicious” activity.
summary: The White House national cyber director was fired after a wave of technology outages. The director’s role includes advising the president on cybersecurity policy, information security, data protection and deterrence of "malicious" activity.
author: Euronews

title: Experts worry as HMS Vengeance completes 217‑day underwater patrol
content: The Royal Navy’s nuclear submarine HMS Vengeance completed a 217‑day underwater patrol, setting a new record for the longest mission of its kind. During the roughly seven‑month deployment, the crew had almost no contact with the outside world. The unprecedented duration of the patrol has prompted concerns among experts.
summary: The Royal Navy's HMS Vengeance nuclear submarine set a new record by completing a 217‑day mission. The crew had almost no contact with the outside world for about seven months.
author: Euronews

title: Lewis Pugh completes 15km Strait of Hormuz swim to expose war’s environmental toll
content:
British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh completed a 15‑kilometre swim through the Strait of Hormuz over three days in November 2026, braving explosions and burning tankers nearby.  

His challenge was designed to expose the environmental damage caused by the war with Iran.
summary: British endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh completed a 15‑kilometre swim through the Strait of Hormuz over three days in November 2026, while explosions and burning tankers occurred nearby. His three‑day challenge was intended to expose the environmental damage caused by the war with Iran.
author: Euronews

title: Mexico arrests FBI most-wanted cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, sparks violence
content: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, identified as one of the FBI’s ten most‑wanted fugitives, was arrested in a military operation in northern Mexico that involved U.S. intelligence cooperation. The raid was followed by gunfire, burning vehicles and panic among civilians.
summary: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s ten most-wanted fugitives, was arrested in a military operation involving US intelligence cooperation. Gunfire, burning vehicles and panic among civilians followed the raid in northern Mexico.
author: Euronews

title: COP31 talks overrun schedule as countries race to finalize climate deal
content: COP31 climate talks have overrun their schedule as countries race to agree on a new global climate deal, following criticism of an earlier draft that made no mention of fossil fuels. The EU has warned that the current proposal risks turning the summit into a “fossil fuel summit”, as negotiators work towards a revised, potentially final agreement expected later today. France 24 International affairs editor Jamie Smith-Maillet tells us more.
summary: COP31 talks overrun schedule as countries race to finalize climate deal.
author: France 24

title: France protests lose momentum as sixth week of demonstrations sees lower turnout
content:
Around 2,200 people participated in protests across France by 2 p.m. local time, the Interior Ministry said, noting 44 demonstrations nationwide and seven arrests while describing the overall situation as generally calm. Turnout was lower than on previous Saturdays, indicating a decline in participation as the movement entered its sixth week.

FRANCE 24’s Antonia Kerrigan reported from Place de la République in Paris that rent‑rights organisations joined the sixth consecutive Saturday of protests. Demonstrations also occurred in seven European countries—including Spain, Portugal, Greece and Germany—where rising living costs and access to affordable housing are key concerns.
summary: Around 2,200 people participated in 44 protests across France on Saturday, with seven arrests and a generally calm situation, according to the Interior Ministry. Rent‑rights groups also joined the sixth consecutive Saturday of demonstrations, which spread to seven European countries such as Spain, Portugal, Greece and Germany over concerns about living costs and affordable housing.
author: France 24

title: Endurance athlete swims in polluted Strait of Hormuz to protest conflict
content: The Strait of Hormuz remains largely blocked, with Iran attacking vessels attempting to cross it, and concerns are rising about the war’s environmental impact as toxic chemicals spread through the air and sea. In response, a swimmer and ocean advocate entered the polluted and dangerous waters of the strait. By plunging into the water, he called on all parties involved to end the conflict.
summary: An endurance athlete and ocean advocate swam in the polluted and dangerous waters of the Strait of Hormuz. He called on all sides to end the conflict as the strait remains largely blocked and Iran attacks vessels attempting to cross.
author: France 24

title: Former rideshare driver Jonathan Rinderknecht convicted of starting 2025 Palisades fire
content: A Los Angeles County jury on Friday found former rideshare driver Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of starting the 2025 Palisades fire, which caused widespread destruction and loss of life. He now faces a prison term of five to 40 years. Liza Kaminov has more.
summary: A Los Angeles County jury found former rideshare driver Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty on Friday of starting the 2025 Palisades fire. He faces a prison sentence of between five and 40 years.
author: France 24

title: FBI investigates major cyberattack on NCIC criminal database
content: The FBI is investigating a reported major cyberattack targeting its national law enforcement database, the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which holds sensitive criminal justice records, including information on fugitives, missing persons, criminal histories and stolen property. President Donald Trump said he had just been briefed on the incident, describing it as “not good”. FRANCE 24’s Fraser Jackson reports from Washington DC.
summary: The FBI is investigating a reported major cyberattack on its National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database, which holds sensitive criminal justice records. President Donald Trump said he had just been briefed on the incident and described it as “not good”, according to FRANCE 24’s Fraser Jackson in Washington DC.
author: France 24

title: COP31 deep divisions over energy, finance and science persist
content:
COP31 climate talks in Turkey have entered overtime as deep divisions over fossil‑fuel policy, climate finance and global‑warming targets have stalled progress toward an agreement. A revised draft that omits any reference to fossil fuels has drawn strong criticism from the European Union and about a dozen other countries, which are calling for an explicit commitment to phase out those fuels.

Negotiators remain split on a proposed global electrification target, carbon‑capture measures and the future of United Nations climate‑science reports. Developing nations have expressed anger over the removal of a $120 billion climate‑adaptation funding target, while Australia is racing to secure a revised deal before the delegates depart, according to France 24 journalist Adria Rocha Cutiller.
summary: COP31 climate talks in Turkey have gone into overtime, with deep divisions over fossil fuels, climate finance and global warming targets delaying an agreement. A revised draft dropped all mention of fossil fuels, prompting strong criticism from the EU and a dozen countries demanding a clear commitment to phase them out.
author: France 24

title: Drone strike ignites Russian cargo ship in Gulf of Finland
content: A Russian cargo ship was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, igniting a fire that caused the vessel to drift into Finnish waters. According to FRANCE 24’s Gulliver Cragg, reporting from Kyiv, the ship is linked to a major Russian military logistics company. Ukrainian officials have not confirmed or denied involvement, a pattern noted by the reporter, while analysts referenced by Cragg say the targeting has an apparent motive.
summary: A Russian cargo ship was hit by drones in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. The vessel is affiliated with a major Russian military logistics company, and Ukrainian authorities have neither confirmed nor denied responsibility, analysts say.
author: France 24

title: EU Council President Antonio Costa proposes smaller 2028-2034 budget with 3% tech tax
content: European Council President Antonio Costa has put forward a reduced EU budget for the 2028‑2034 period that incorporates a 3 % levy on major digital firms intended to lower member‑state contributions. France has already rejected the proposal, describing it as inadequate.
summary: European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034 that includes a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has rejected the plan as inadequate.
author: DW World

title: EU and Indonesia sign trade deal covering 730 million people, lowering tariffs
content: The European Union and Indonesia have signed a trade agreement that will affect 730 million people. The pact promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities, reflecting the EU’s aim to diversify its trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.
summary: The European Union and Indonesia have signed a trade agreement that covers 730 million people. The deal promises lower tariffs and new investment opportunities as the EU seeks to diversify trade ties amid growing global economic tensions.
author: DW World

title: Russian helicopter suspected of breaching Finnish airspace, linked to drone strike
content: Finland’s Defense Ministry says a Russian helicopter suspected of breaching Finnish airspace may be connected to a drone strike that occurred on Saturday against a Russian cargo ship. The cargo vessel targeted in the strike is listed on a United States sanctions list.
summary: A Russian helicopter is suspected of violating Finnish airspace. Finland's Defense Ministry believes the incursion is connected to a drone strike on a Russian cargo ship, which is on a US sanctions list, that occurred earlier Saturday.
author: DW World

title: UN Secretary-General Guterres to co‑host AI safety summit in Barbados
content: UN Secretary‑General António Guterres will travel to Barbados on Monday to co‑host a special artificial‑intelligence safety summit in Bridgetown. The meeting is intended to address the widening gap between rapidly increasing AI risks and the limited capacity of many countries to keep pace with the technology’s development.
summary: UN Secretary-General António Guterres is heading to Barbados to co‑host a special summit on artificial intelligence (AI) safety on Monday. The summit aims to close the gap between accelerating risks and many countries’ capacity to deal with the pace of development.
author: UN News

title: Haiti’s farmers rebuild amid gang violence, hunger and El Niño impacts
content: Haitian farmers are attempting to rebuild their livelihoods as homes remain abandoned and harvests fail, a situation linked to ongoing violence, hunger and the effects of El Niño. Years of insecurity, gang‑driven violence, economic instability, displacement, poor agricultural performance and climate shocks have left millions of Haitians struggling to meet their food needs.
summary: Years of insecurity, gang violence, economic instability, displacement, poor agricultural performance and climate shocks have left millions of Haitians struggling to meet their food needs. Haiti’s farmers are attempting to rebuild their homes and harvests despite the ongoing violence, hunger and El Niño conditions.
author: UN News

title: Manchester’s Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge revive reggae sound system culture
content:
Manchester‑based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have revitalised the local music scene, creating a sense of belonging and empowerment for community members. Their work has helped to revive the sound system culture that has long been a cornerstone of Manchester’s nightlife and identity.

For a generation of young Black Mancunians, the lessons that mattered most were not taught in classrooms but through towering stacks of amps, speakers, turntables and Jamaican records. “We didn’t know where we fit in. We didn’t know our history. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge. He notes that records by Burning Spear, Bob Marley and Culture were telling them about their culture, something that was not part of the school curriculum.

According to Beaumont, the sound system was not merely entertainment; it served as an education, providing a cultural narrative that filled gaps left by formal schooling.
summary: Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the reggae sound system culture, offering belonging and empowerment to young Black Mancunians. Founder member Errol “Barzy” Beaumont says the records and sound system taught them about their culture, which was absent from school curricula.
author: Guardian World

title: Reform UK weighs pact with Restore Britain ahead of Castle Bromwich byelection
content:
A byelection in Castle Bromwich, held on Thursday in the West Midlands, is the latest test for Reform UK.  The vote comes at a time when the party’s support is seen as vulnerable, with the Conservatives edging ahead in recent polls.  

Reform UK has said it is considering a pact with Restore Britain to address its stalling performance.  Restore Britain, a hard‑right party founded by Rupert Lowe after a split with Nigel Farage, could play a decisive role in the upcoming election.
summary: Reform UK is considering a pact with the hard‑right party Restore Britain to address its stalled poll performance. The Thursday Castle Bromwich byelection in the West Midlands is being viewed as a test for Reform UK while Conservatives are edging ahead in recent polls.
author: Guardian World

title: Princess of Wales discusses cancer impact in BBC documentary Heal
content: Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’ The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month. “Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”
summary: The BBC documentary "Heal" features Princess of Wales Catherine, 44, speaking about how her cancer diagnosis changes her physically and deeply emotionally. It also shows her taking on the Three Peaks challenge, expressing a sense of hope alongside uncertainty, and will air later this month.
author: Guardian World

title: UK cold turns to rain; Met Office warns of 100mm+ on Dartmoor
content:
Cold weather is set to be replaced by heavy rain in parts of the United Kingdom after the Met Office issued a weather warning for south‑west England. The warning covers a slow‑moving band of rain that will cross Devon and Cornwall, with forecasts calling for more than 100 mm of rain to fall on Dartmoor.

Flood alerts have been activated and there is a risk of power cuts as the rain is expected to begin at 6 a.m. on Sunday and continue until midnight.
summary: The Met Office issued a weather warning for south‑west England as a slow‑moving band of rain will bring more than 100 mm to Dartmoor on Sunday. Flood alerts are in place and there is a risk of power cuts, with the warning running from 6 am to midnight.
author: Guardian World

title: Barnham village votes to ‘leave the UK’ over plan to house 930 asylum seekers
content: Local MP says legitimate criticisms of asylum housing plans are being co-opted by opposition parties ‘stirring up racial discord’ Residents of a Suffolk village have voted to “leave the UK” in a referendum held in response to government plans to house 930 asylum seekers at a nearby former military base. Approximately 500 people in Barnham were eligible to take part in the symbolic vote on Saturday. There were 257 votes for independence, 16 against and one spoiled ballot.
summary: Barnham village votes to ‘leave the UK’ over plan to house 930 asylum seekers.
author: Guardian World

title: British father Joshua Foster fined €3,000 after son falls from Cyprus hotel window
content:
British father Joshua Foster has described the “despair” he felt when his two‑year‑old son slipped from his grasp and fell from a fourth‑storey hotel window in Cyprus during a family holiday. Foster said he “lost control” of the child at the moment of the fall.

He later pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Cypriot prosecutors, who had refused to drop the case, imposed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty on Foster.
summary: Joshua Foster said he “lost control” of his two‑year‑old son when the child fell from a fourth‑floor hotel window in Cyprus. He pleaded guilty to causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was ordered to pay a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after prosecutors refused to drop the case.
author: Guardian World

title: UN CCW talks on autonomous weapons collapse after Russian objections
content: Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’ Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections. Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
summary: UN CCW talks on autonomous weapons collapse after Russian objections.
author: Guardian World

title: Mexican military arrests FBI top fugitive Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in Sinaloa raid
content: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s top 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night. Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.
summary: The Mexican military captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, during a special forces raid in the state of Sinaloa on Friday night. He was arrested with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.
author: Guardian World

title: SpaceX launches classified US Space Force mission from California
content:
SpaceX carried out a classified launch for the U.S. Space Force on November 20, 2026. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 04:20 GMT on November 21). The mission, designated USSF‑317, sent an undisclosed payload into orbit from California’s central coast.

The Falcon 9’s first stage separated roughly 8.5 minutes after liftoff and returned to the Pacific Ocean, landing on the SpaceX drone ship “Of Course I Still Love You.” This was the 11th launch and landing for booster B1100, which now rests on the deck of the drone ship following the USSF‑317 launch. SpaceX concluded its launch webcast shortly after the touchdown, so the upper stage’s ascent to orbit was not televised.

USSF‑317 is a classified mission, so the upper stage’s cargo and destination are not publicly known. Some experts suggest the payload could be a group of SpaceX’s Starshield satellites, which would support the Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio and help the military monitor potential targets worldwide.

The 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026, USSF‑317 is the third SpaceX mission for the Space Force in November. Most of this year’s Falcon 9 flights—about 70 %—have focused on expanding SpaceX’s Starlink low‑Earth‑orbit internet constellation, which now contains more than 11,000 satellites. The company has flown 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, but plans to retire the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy in favor of the fully reusable Starship megare‑rocket, which has already deployed 26 next‑generation Starlink V3 satellites on its latest test flights.
summary: SpaceX launches classified US Space Force mission from California.
author: Space.com

title: ESA-JAXA BepiColombo probe begins Mercury orbit insertion today
content:
BepiColombo, the joint European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission, entered orbit around Mercury today, November 21. The spacecraft will begin its orbit‑insertion burn at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT), a 37‑minute maneuver that will place the probe into the planet’s gravitational field.

The mission comprises ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also called Mio. Both orbiter modules were launched together with the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018. The MTM released MPO and Mio on September 3, and the two spacecraft remain connected until about December 9, when they will separate.

BepiColombo’s journey to Mercury involved one Earth flyby, two Venus flybys, and six Mercury flybys over roughly seven years—a duration extended by a year after a solar‑panel issue reduced power for the MTM’s electric thrusters. The arrival phase, lasting about six months, is now complete. Mio will settle into a highly elliptical polar orbit over Mercury’s poles, while MPO will perform engine burns before reaching its own polar orbit on March 10, 2027.

Science operations will commence on April 6, 2027. ESA officials describe the mission as a comprehensive study of Mercury’s magnetosphere, its interaction with the solar wind, internal structure—including a large iron core—and the origin of its magnetic field. The data are expected to deepen understanding of the planet’s formation and the evolution of the inner solar system.
summary: Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov.
author: Space.com

title: LIV Golf Liquidation Begins as Saudi Support Ends
content:
LIV Golf is heading toward bankruptcy court and liquidation proceedings scheduled to begin in January 2027, marking the end of the professional golf tour. Jonathan Liew notes the irony that the venture, originally championed by Greg Norman amidst human rights concerns, was ultimately dismantled by the Saudi government. Liew references Norman’s previous comment about learning from mistakes and moving forward, applying it to LIV’s current trajectory toward financial collapse.

The article highlights the final seven months of LIV’s decline, which began when Saudi Arabia stopped funding the organization. Consequently, LIV’s chief executive, Scott O’Neil, was compelled to seek new investors in midtown Manhattan. Liew describes O’Neil’s efforts as "panhandling for change," noting that he presented conceptual revenue forecasts while attempting to portray the tour as a legitimate business with a viable future and profit potential.
summary: LIV Golf has entered liquidation proceedings scheduled for January 2027 after Saudi Arabia withdrew its funding. LIV’s chief executive Scott O’Neil has reportedly panicked, panhandling in Manhattan and presenting fictional revenue forecasts.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Scotland smashed by Swiss; Mauricio Pochettino takes charge
content: Max Rushden joins Barry Glendenning, Ali Maxwell, Dan Bardell, and Ewan Murray for a Football Weekly video segment. The discussion covers the recent international break, noting that Scotland was defeated by Switzerland and that Mauricio Pochettino has taken charge. The panel also previews the upcoming Premier League weekend, specifically highlighting the match between Liverpool and Manchester United.
summary: Scotland were smashed by the Swiss, and Mauricio Pochettino has taken charge. Max Rushden, Barry Glendenning, Ali Maxwell, Dan Bardell and Ewan Murray wrap up the latest international break and preview the Premier League weekend, including Liverpool v Manchester United.
author: Guardian Sport

title: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani Sidelined Nine Months With Achilles Tear
content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a lifelong Arsenal supporter, has sustained an Achilles tear that will sideline him for nine months. The injury occurred during a friendly soccer match with the press corps on Thursday. This news adds to the recent setbacks for the Gunners, following the announcement that player Bukayo Saka may not return to action before Christmas due to an ongoing thigh injury rehabilitation.

Mamdani detailed the circumstances of his injury during a press conference, which initially focused on his administration’s plans to close the Rikers Island jail complex. The revelation of his extended absence from soccer activity highlights a significant personal setback for the mayor, who is described as one of Arsenal’s most famous supporters. The confirmation of his nine-month recovery period underscores the severity of the Achilles tear sustained during the friendly match.
summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tore his Achilles tendon during a friendly soccer match on Thursday. He is expected to be out of action for nine months until next summer.

title: Kane vows return after ankle surgery as Premier League resumes
content:
Harry Kane has vowed to return to action following ankle surgery, as the Premier League resumes its schedule. The news cycle also features a reader contribution from Patrick Morgan addressing the perceived decline of traditional wingers in modern football. Morgan argues that the shift is tactical rather than a lack of talent, citing Arsenal’s current system as an example.

According to Morgan, players such as Calafiori, Timber, and White often operate in the half-space or tuck into midfield, requiring wide players to function more like No 8s. He notes that Saka is an exception who performs both roles, while much of Arsenal’s dynamism stems from Declan Rice’s central play. Morgan contrasts this with the 2015–2020 era, when wingers were given more license to stay forward. He concludes by expressing a preference for Alexis Sánchez, highlighting his record of 60 goals in 120 league games and his musical abilities.
summary: Harry Kane vowed to return after undergoing ankle surgery as the Premier League resumed. The news roundup also included a reader's tactical analysis of Arsenal's wide players and a tribute to Alexis Sánchez.

title: Panama’s minister warns COP31 not to ignore objections as conference runs into overtime
content:
COP31 has extended into overtime as negotiations on the final cover text remain unresolved. On Friday night, COP President Murat Kurum approved several less controversial agenda items but instructed governments to remain at the venue until midnight in case his team required consultations. He noted that the cover text remained in its Thursday version and advised delegates to rest if they were not contacted, suggesting they need not return before 9 a.m. Saturday. Consequently, the conference centre was largely empty on Saturday morning. At approximately 12:30 p.m., Kurum told Swedish TV station SVT that the conference was attempting to reach consensus and expected more effort from parties, stating that a conclusion might take shape in the afternoon.

Tensions surfaced during Friday night’s plenary session, where an activist was removed by security after holding a rope around his neck and shouting that leaders were killing the future. Separately, Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro urged Kurum to fully respect the rules of procedure when making decisions over the weekend. Navarro, who has previously threatened to object to the cover text if it lacked sufficient ambition, issued this warning to ensure that objections are not ignored, a practice for which previous COP presidents have faced criticism.

Another significant development occurred on Friday night with a joint statement from Australia and China. The statement included China’s backing for the 35×35 electrification goal. Meanwhile, negotiations regarding the Just Transition Mechanism failed to achieve sufficient progress to operationalize the body. The latest draft text, issued on Thursday, presented three options after earlier versions drew criticism from civil society for offering limited outcomes such as reports and dialogues.

Developing countries and civil society favored an option for a functioning body that would work with governments, organizations, and affected communities outside the UN climate process. However, observers reported that this option was rejected by the EU, UK, and Norway. Developing countries also opposed a second option that would merely establish a contact group to coordinate efforts and a rolling five-year work plan. This lack of progress is notable because the Just Transition Mechanism had made advances during June’s Bonn talks, where an informal note compiled various proposals and raised hopes for its establishment in Türkiye.

Approximately 700 organizations representing workers, Indigenous people, women, and youth issued a letter during COP31 calling for a mechanism that advances human and labor rights and provides decent work during the transition to a low-carbon world. Despite these efforts, developed countries have been unwilling to accept what they view as new obligations or sources of financial demand. Some just transition experts indicate it is preferable to continue discussions over the coming year to establish the mechanism at COP32 in Addis Ababa on a stronger basis, while others fear it may not be realized. Sinéad Magner, just transition lead for the Women and Gender Constituency, warned that pushing the issue out for another year could effectively kill it through incremental delays.
summary: Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro warned COP31 president Murat Kurum not to ignore objections and urged full respect of procedural rules during the conference's overtime sessions. The Just Transition Mechanism was stalled, with negotiations failing to reach agreement before COP31 closed.
author: Climate Home News

title: COP31 set for disaster as EU blocks climate finance and omits fossil fuel language
content: Brandon Wu oversees research, advocacy, coalition building and campaigning work for ActionAid USA. “Fossil fuels dumped from latest draft deal at climate summit.” “Ambition goes missing as fossil fuel language drops from draft deal.” “Anger as COP31 draft climate deal removes all mentions of fossil fuels.” These are a few selected headlines about the COP31 climate negotiations as they draw to a close this weekend – and they all miss the point. Yes, the UN climate negotiations should address fossil fuels, the primary driver of the climate crisis. But there are many other key issues at play in the negotiations. Yes, COP31 is shaping up to be a disastrous failure for people and the planet, especially frontline communities in the Global South. But it’s because of much more than the absence of language on fossil fuel phaseout. COP31 Bulletin Day 11: Countries decry cover text for omitting fossil fuels The UN climate negotiations are premised on the idea that the countries of the Global North, which have built their wealth on the backs of heavily polluting fossil fuel-based economies, must do two main things: reduce their emissions and provide support for poorer countries of the Global South. Enabled by climate finance from the Global North, Global South countries should transition much faster to clean, sustainable economies than they would be able to do otherwise. In addition, given their climate inaction of the past many decades – including ongoing and, in some cases, increasing use of fossil fuels – those Global North countries must also pay to support adaptation to future climate impacts, as well as to respond to loss and damage from climate shocks and stresses that have already happened. Bad-faith negotiating On August 26, catastrophic warming-driven glacial floods hit Nepal, with some 1,500 people dead and over 5,000 still missing. Almost exactly two months later, EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said that any new pledges for climate finance to support countries like Nepal were “dead in the water.” This comment was shocking for how callous and tone-deaf it was. But it was also shocking because it was the EU openly declaring that they were coming to the COP31 negotiations with nothing to offer – that they would have no intent to negotiate in good faith. Without finance from rich developed countries, the UN climate regime simply does not, and cannot, work. This is the real story of the failure of COP31. The actual negotiating deliverables for this year’s climate summit include a work programme on climate finance, an institution to support countries to design just transition plans, and progress on adaptation goals supported by adaptation finance. Across all of these negotiating tracks, developed countries led by the EU have done nothing but bullying and blocking. It is deeply unfair and incoherent for developed countries to call for quicker fossil fuel phaseout in poorer countries while denying those countries the support they need to deliver. This position becomes even more nonsensical when considering that developed countries’ claims to “leadership” on fossil fuel phaseout are built on lies. The “roadmaps” for transitioning away from fossil fuels that some of these countries have announced are nothing more than repackaged existing policies – exercises in public relations rather than serious plans for change. Ugandan oil official welcomes transition roadmap as nation gears up for exports Why the broader story matters A singular focus on the lack of fossil fuel outcomes – which were not actually on the agenda for the COP31 negotiations – conveniently blurs the story of EU and Global North bad faith out of the picture. It allows the rich countries to do their usual blame game, pointing the finger at Saudi Arabia and similar countries (ignoring the fact that it is actually the United States that has, by far, the world’s largest oil and gas expansion plans). A political signal in the COP31 text reiterating the importance of phasing out fossil fuels would be very useful (though it would be deeply undermined by language around carbon capture and storage that does exist in the text and must be removed). But that is not actually what this year’s negotiations are about. Finance, adaptation, and just transition are among the major negotiating tracks at COP31. On each one of these tracks, rich countries have been stonewalling at every turn. Not only are they refusing to fulfill their obligations, they are undermining future obligations and pointing the finger at anyone but themselves when a weak negotiating outcome is the result. We should be outraged at the lack of progress in phasing out fossil fuels, but we cannot lose sight of the real blockers of progress in the broader geopolitics of the UN climate talks. Saying climate finance is “dead in the water” weeks before negotiations even begin? The EU taking up the mantle of climate villain now that the Trump-led US is out of the picture? That’s the real scandal. The post COP31 is shaping up to be a disaster – not only because it’s weak on fossil fuels appeared first on Climate Home News.
summary: EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said new pledges for climate finance to support countries like Nepal were “dead in the water.” COP31 negotiations have omitted fossil fuel language and seen rich countries block progress on finance, adaptation, and just transition, threatening a disastrous outcome for frontline communities.

title: COP31 ends without deal as NGOs warn of disappointing outcome
content: Though the climate talks officially finished on Friday, no final deal was agreed. NGOs are warning that this summit might fall disastrously short of what is needed Although not quite deserted, the halls of the Cop31 conference centre are considerably less peopled today. A few people wander back and forth with their backpacks on. Young Turkish support staff walk around in groups. It’s possible to find a seat at the tables next to the food stalls. Those, however, are closed, so there is nothing to actually rest on the table except for your laptop.
summary: The COP31 climate talks officially concluded on Friday without a final agreement. NGOs warned the summit could fall disastrously short of what is needed, and the conference centre was notably less crowded.

title: Over 1 billion people worldwide suffer preventable vision loss due to limited care
content: More than 1 billion people worldwide live with vision loss, many because they lack the glasses needed for clear sight, while others are affected by cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration or diabetic eye disease. The title identifies uneven access to care as the primary driver of this preventable condition.
summary: More than 1 billion people around the world live with vision loss. Many lack needed glasses, while others have cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration or diabetic eye disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: University of Bath study finds transgender consumers face discrimination in services
content: New research from the University of Bath finds that transgender consumers may encounter discrimination and psychological harm while performing routine activities. The study highlights challenges in tasks such as changing a name, using a gym, and accessing banking and health‑care services.
summary: New research from the University of Bath finds that transgender consumers can experience discrimination and psychological harm when carrying out everyday tasks. The study cites examples such as changing a name, visiting a gym, and accessing banking and health care.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Custom MRI tool may detect pancreatic cancer chemo response within weeks
content:
About 60 % of people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer are ineligible for surgery because their disease is too advanced. For these patients, treatment usually starts with chemotherapy in the hope that the tumor will shrink enough to become operable, as surgery offers the best chance of long‑term survival.

The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center—Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute has launched a clinical trial of a custom MRI imaging tool. The tool is intended to detect, within weeks, whether chemotherapy is effective, allowing clinicians to adjust treatment promptly if it is not.
summary: About 60% of people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer don't qualify for surgery because their disease is too advanced. For these patients, treatment typically begins with chemotherapy, in the hope that the tumor will shrink enough to be surgically removed, which offers the best chance of long-term survival.
author: Medical Xpress

title: One in five Americans with mental health conditions face treatment options unchanged since 1950s
content: One in five Americans lives with a mental health condition, and the range of treatments available to them has changed little since the mid‑20th century. Most psychiatric medications in use today were first developed in the 1950s, according to the source.
summary: One in five Americans have a mental health condition. Their treatment options have changed little since the 1950s, when most psychiatric medicines were first pioneered.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Liverpool scientists locate protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy
content: Cell biologists at the University of Liverpool have identified the intracellular location of a protein associated with a severe form of childhood epilepsy. The finding clarifies how the protein is positioned within nerve cells and offers new insight into the underlying mechanisms of this rare genetic neurological disorder.
summary: University of Liverpool scientists have discovered how a protein linked to a severe form of childhood epilepsy is positioned within nerve cells. The finding provides new insights into the rare genetic neurological disorder.
author: Medical Xpress

title: University of Otago finds New Zealand lacks current data on common gut disorders
content: University of Otago research indicates that New Zealand lacks current research on common gut disorders, creating a major data gap. The absence of up‑to‑date information means the country is “flying blind” on conditions that may affect roughly one‑third of adults.
summary: University of Otago research says New Zealand has no up‑to‑date research on common gut disorders that may affect about one in three adults. The data gap leaves the country effectively flying blind on these conditions.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Health professionals to be upskilled for emotional support of Australians with diabetes
content:
An initiative is set to upskill health professionals so they can provide emotional‑well‑being support to people with diabetes.  

The effort targets more than 1.5 million Australians with diabetes, who manage their condition around the clock, making daily decisions about medication, glucose monitoring, food, physical activity and other aspects of care largely outside the health‑care system.
summary: More than 1.5 million Australians live with diabetes and must manage their condition continuously. Health professionals are being upskilled to provide emotional‑well‑being support for these patients.
author: Medical Xpress

title: New bioinformatics toolkit maps virus‑microbe interactions at planetary scale
content: A new bioinformatics toolkit and accompanying database have been released to enable researchers to link viruses with their natural bacterial and archaeal hosts on a planetary scale. Microbiomes, which consist of bacteria and archaea, are constantly interacting with viruses that can both kill hosts and temporarily confer new capabilities. Because many viruses have not been cultured in laboratories, establishing these host‑virus connections has been challenging; the newly available resources aim to address that gap and expand understanding of microbial‑viral dynamics.
summary: Microbiomes contain bacteria and archaea that constantly interact with and are infected by viruses, which can alter microbiome processes by killing hosts or temporarily granting new capabilities. Researchers now have a new bioinformatics toolkit and database that enable large‑scale association of viruses with their natural hosts.
author: Phys.org

title: Parasite protein reveals new details of mitochondrial ribosome assembly
content:
A parasite protein has provided new insight into the process by which mitochondria assemble their ribosomes, broadening scientific understanding of this aspect of mitochondrial biology.  

Mitochondria are essential organelles in most organisms, including humans, and are commonly described as the cell’s powerhouses because they generate the energy required for cellular functions. They originated from free‑living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells in the distant past.
summary: A parasite protein expands understanding of how mitochondria build their ribosomes. Mitochondria are essential cellular components that produce energy and evolved from free‑living bacteria.
author: Phys.org

title: LLNL scientists improve X‑ray temperature measurements at NIF under extreme pressure
content: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF). This development offers new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high‑energy‑density physics.
summary: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials under extreme pressure at the National Ignition Facility. The work provides new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high‑energy‑density physics.
author: Phys.org

title: Global study shows lakes speed glacier ice loss
content: A new global analysis shows that lakes bordering glaciers can speed glacier retreat. The study notes that lake water can melt ice from beneath the glacier and that ice chunks can calve directly into the lake. Prior research had not clearly quantified how these lake‑related processes compare with other factors influencing glacier ice loss worldwide.
summary: Glacial lakes can accelerate glacier retreat by melting ice from beneath and by causing ice chunks to break off into the lake. A new global analysis has clarified how these lake‑related processes compare with other factors influencing glacier loss.
author: Phys.org

title: People wade through floodwater despite danger, prompting safety advice
content: A footpath can disappear beneath brown floodwater, leaving only a short crossing ahead while a detour would be long and cause lateness. The scenario illustrates how people may wade through water because they underestimate the danger, prompting flood‑safety advice to focus on these everyday decisions.
summary: Some individuals choose to wade across flooded footpaths, believing the crossing is short. Flood safety advice emphasizes the need to recognize the risk of underestimating floodwater.
author: Phys.org

title: UQ students develop prototype to measure strawberry skin strength for breeders
content: University of Queensland engineering students have created a prototype device that measures the strength of strawberry skin. The tool is intended to help the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland’s Department of Primary Industries more readily identify resilient strawberry varieties.
summary: The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin. It was created by University of Queensland engineering students to aid the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries in identifying resilient varieties.
